title: Bucket composting toilet with urine diversion
summary: A waterless toilet from pails, a seat and a funnel that sends urine to its own jug, with sawdust, soil or ash over each deposit and bins where the waste breaks down over a year or more. Kept dry and well covered it barely smells. The danger is treating the result as safe too soon: faeces need long storage or proper hot composting, and never go on food eaten raw.

materials.item: Lidded plastic pails, 19–20 L (5 gal): one in use, spares to swap in
Plywood or boards for a box or bench around the pail, at seat height
Plastic funnel or the top of a cut plastic jug as the urine diverter (no metal)
Plastic hose or pipe from the funnel to the urine jug, with a steady fall
Capped plastic jug or jerry can for urine, 10–20 L, marked URINE, never used for water again
Dry cover material: sawdust, wood shavings, dry soil, or clean wood ash
Compost bins from pallets or boards, with lids
Straw, dry leaves or wood chips for the bins
pH paper, to check ash- or lime-treated material

steps.text: Pick the spot for the bins: on ground that doesn't drain towards a well or water, at least 30 m (100 ft) from a dug well and 15 m (50 ft) from a drilled well, lake or stream: those are Ontario's legal minimums (TBDHU). Where you can, keep 30 m from every well and water, as in [Latrines and distances](#ref/reference_sanitation/latrines_and_distances).
Build a box or bench that holds the pail under the seat, with the seat at a normal toilet height and the pail easy to slide out.

Fit the urine diverter at the front of the seat opening: a funnel or cut jug that catches urine and drains through a hose with a steady fall into the capped urine jug. Faeces must not drop into it, and urine must not splash back into the pail (Compendium).
Run the hose down close to the bottom of the jug and seal round it, so urine doesn't spray and smell stays in (Compendium). Use plastic, not metal: urine corrodes most metals (Compendium).

Put a layer of cover material in the bottom of the empty pail. After every use, cover the faeces with a scoop of sawdust, dry soil, ash or lime (Compendium). Use more when anyone has diarrhoea (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5).
steps.warn: Lime burns skin and eyes, especially when damp. Use gloves and goggles, and keep it away from children.

steps.text: Keep water out of the pail. Wipe the seat and funnel with a damp cloth instead of pouring water in (Compendium). Close the lid after each use.
Empty the urine jug before it's full: onto soil away from water, or onto your own plants as fertiliser (see notes). In frost, keep it indoors or empty it daily.
steps.warn: Never put bleach in the urine jug or funnel. Stored urine gives off ammonia (Compendium), and bleach with ammonia makes a toxic gas.

steps.text: When a pail is nearly full, put its lid on and swap in a clean one. Empty full pails into the active bin and cover with straw, leaves or wood chips.

Empty the pail into the bin, wipe it out with a damp cloth rather than rinsing it with a lot of water, and let it dry before reuse. Wear gloves, and wash hands with soap afterwards (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5, CDC workers).

Check the bin's moisture now and then: a gloved handful should leave only a few drops of water, neither crumbling dry nor dripping like a wet sponge. If it's too wet, add more dry material (Compendium).

When a bin is full, cap it with dry material and a lid, and start the next. Leave the full one alone for the time in the notes: 1.5 to 2 years if it never gets hot (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5). That time removes most bacteria and cuts viruses and parasites a good deal, but not all of them (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5).

Use the finished material around ornamental trees, shrubs and flowers, worked into the soil. Keep it off vegetables, fruit, berries and root crops eaten raw, and away from fruit trees and berry bushes whose fruit is eaten raw (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5).
steps.warn: Never put it on vegetables, fruit or root crops eaten raw, and stop any use at least a month before harvest (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5).

notes:
## What this toilet is, honestly

A bucket toilet that keeps urine and faeces apart and covers each deposit with dry material. It uses no water and, kept dry, has little smell. The bins downstream do the slow work of making the waste safer.

Most composting chambers don't reliably reach the heat that sanitising compost needs (Compendium). A study of end-product from 16 public composting toilets at 12 sites in western North America found that ammonia from urine inhibited microbial activity yet was not enough to sanitise the end-product (Hill 2013, read from the EPA record's title and abstract, not the paper). So keep urine out, give the bins time, and treat the product with care.

In cold climates a composting chamber needs to be indoors, or the cold stops the microbes (Compendium). In Canada an outdoor bin is frozen for months, and breakdown stops below zero (WEDC Guide 29). In winter, store full pails as in [toilets in winter](#guides/skill_toilets_in_winter) and add them to the bins in spring.

## Planning numbers

| What | About | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Urine | 1.2 L a person a day | Compendium |
| Urine | 500 L a person a year | EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 6 |
| Faeces | 50 L a person a year | EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 6 |
| Composting chamber size | 300 L a person a year | Compendium |
| Drying vault size | 50 L a person every 6 months | Compendium |

Keeping urine out removes most of the volume and most of the smell.

## Cover material

- **What:** sawdust, wood shavings, dry soil, ash or lime after every use; wood chips, straw, paper or leaves in the bins (Compendium).
- **Why:** ash and lime lower the moisture and raise the pH, which makes conditions hard for germs and cuts smell and flies (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5). Wet faeces let bacteria survive and multiply and start to stink (Compendium).
- **Ash:** only from clean wood. Never ash from trash, cardboard, coal, charcoal or painted or treated wood: see [Lye from wood ash](#ref/reference_chemicals/lye_from_wood_ash).
- **Lime** is caustic: see [Lime, wet cement and lye](#browse/hazards/caustic).
- **Winter:** lay in a winter's supply in autumn and keep it dry indoors.

## The urine side

- Urine normally leaves the body free of germs, but faeces can get into it (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 6).
- **For your own household's plants** you can use it straight away. Put it on close to the ground, work it in, and stop at least a month before harvest (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5).
- **Urine shared between households** is stored first: 1 to 6 months at 4–20 °C, undiluted, in a sealed container, depending on the crop (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5). Storage over 6 months makes it nearly germ-free (Compendium).
- **How much:** a rough rule is one person's urine for a day on 1 m² of crop for the season (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 6).
- **Not needed as fertiliser:** pour it onto soil well away from water, or into a soak pit more than 30 m from drinking water and 2 m above the groundwater (Compendium). Frozen ground won't take it in; pour it where meltwater won't carry it to a well or stream.
- **Cleaning:** scale builds up in the funnel and hose. Mild vinegar or hot water stops it (Compendium). Never follow vinegar with bleach, or bleach with vinegar: see [Never mix](#ref/reference_chemicals/never_mix).

## Bins and time

Use two or three bins and fill one at a time. In a single bin the top is always fresh, so emptying it is riskier (Compendium).

A bin works best with plenty of air, 45 to 70 % moisture and enough carbon (straw, sawdust, leaves) to balance the nitrogen. Turn it now and then (Compendium). The squeeze test in step 10 checks moisture.

| Treatment | How long | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Hot composting | All of it at 50 °C or more for at least 7 days, turned so the edges get hot too | EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5 |
| Storage at 2–20 °C | 1.5 to 2 years | EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5, Compendium |
| Storage, warmer than 20 °C on average | About 1 year | EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5 |
| Ash or lime, held above pH 9 | At least 6 months | EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5 |

- A thermometer pushed into the middle of the pile tells you whether it really got hot. Without one, assume it didn't. The Compendium treats 50 °C for a week as the least before compost counts as safe to use, says reaching it takes much longer than a week of composting, and elsewhere aims for 2 to 4 months at 55 to 60 °C (Compendium).
- The storage times are for places where the temperature reaches up to about 20 °C (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5). In much of Canada an outdoor bin spends months frozen, when breakdown stops (WEDC Guide 29), so the times above may fall short. As a cautious rule of our own, not a figure from the sources, take 2 years as the least, and longer if the bin was frozen for most of it. The Compendium's 1.5 to 2 years is for dried faeces kept dry; wet material may need longer.
- pH paper tells you whether ash or lime is holding the pH above 9. EcoSanRes says a pH over 9 for 6 months kills most pathogens, and that adding chemicals is mainly an option in large systems with trained staff, so don't count on a few scoops of ash to get a household bin there (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5).

## Using the finished material

- Work it well into the soil; don't leave it on the surface (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5).
- **Never** on vegetables, fruit or root crops eaten raw. At least one month between the last use and harvest, for urine and for treated faeces (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5).
- If in doubt, compost it longer, or bury it in a pit and plant an ornamental tree in the soil above it, not in the waste (Compendium). Dig the pit well away from wells and water and above the high water table: see [Latrines and distances](#ref/reference_sanitation/latrines_and_distances).
- Ornamental trees, shrubs, flower beds and firewood lots carry the least risk, not none: after the full storage time some viruses and parasites can survive and a low risk remains (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5, Compendium). Keep it away from fruit trees and berry bushes whose fruit is eaten raw.
- Dry material can blow as dust. Wear gloves and covering clothes, and don't let it blow into your face (Compendium).

## Siting and rules

Ontario counts composting toilets and pail privies as Class 1 sewage systems, with the same setbacks as a pit privy: 15 m from a drilled well, 30 m from a dug well, 15 m from a lake or stream (TBDHU). Keep the faeces in containers above ground that don't leak into the soil (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5). Liquid draining from a bin carries germs (Compendium): keep bins off ground that drains towards water or floods. More distances are in [Latrines and distances](#ref/reference_sanitation/latrines_and_distances).

## Problems

| Problem | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Smell | Too wet, or urine getting into the pail | More cover; check the funnel lines up (Compendium) |
| Flies | Faeces not covered | Cover every time; ash helps (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5) |
| Urine jug freezes or splits | Left in the cold | Keep it indoors in frost, or empty it daily |
| Funnel or hose blocked | Mineral scale | Vinegar or hot water (Compendium) |

Put a hand-washing station by the toilet: see [the tippy tap](#guides/build_tippy_tap) and [Handwashing](#ref/reference_sanitation/handwashing).

sources.title: Compendium: Compendium of Sanitation Systems and Technologies, 2nd revised edition (Tilley and others, Eawag, 2014): U.2 Urine-diverting dry toilet, S.1 Urine storage, S.7 Dehydration vaults, S.8 Composting chamber, D.3, D.4, D.7
EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 5: Guidelines for the safe use of urine and faeces in ecological sanitation systems (Stockholm Environment Institute, 2005)
EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 6: Guidelines on the use of urine and faeces in crop production (Stockholm Environment Institute, 2005)

Hill 2013: Hill, Baldwin and Vinnerås, Composting toilets a misnomer: excessive ammonia from urine inhibits microbial activity yet is insufficient in sanitizing the end-product, Journal of Environmental Management 119 (2013), US EPA HERO record
WEDC Guide 29: Pit latrines for special circumstances (Bob Reed, WEDC, Loughborough University, 2014), cold climates
TBDHU: Thunder Bay District Health Unit, A practical guide to Class 1 sewage systems (pit privy), with Ontario Building Code requirements (revised 2016)
CDC workers: Protecting workers handling human waste (2024)
